(CNN) -- Around 200 new species of frogs have been found in Madagascar, one of the world's biodiversity hotspots. A study has found nearly 200 new species of frogs in Madagascar. A study identified between 129 and 221 new species of frogs on the island. The Spanish Scientific Research Council (CSIC), who carried out the study, believe the find could practically double the number of amphibians known in the world if the results are extrapolated at a global scale. The study, published in the journal "Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the USA," suggests that the number of amphibian species in Madagascar has been significantly underestimated. "The diversity of species in Madagascar is far from being known and there is still a lot of scientific research to be done. Our data suggest that the number of new species of amphibians not only has been underestimated but it is spatially widespread, even in well studied areas," said Professor David R. Vieites, CSIC researcher to the press at the Spanish National Natural Sciences Museum in Madrid. "For example, two of the most visited and studied national parks, Ranomafana and Mantadía/Analamazaotra, harbor 31 and 10 new species respectively." Dr. Frank Glaw, curator of herpetology at the Zoologische Staatssammlung from Munich was part of the research team: "During the past 15 years, we discovered and described over 100 new frog species from Madagascar, which led us to believe that our species inventory is almost complete. But as our new surveys show, there are many more species than we suspected," he said in a press statement. The paper suggests that the total biodiversity on the island could be much higher in other species as well, so the actual destruction of natural habitats may be affecting more animals than previously thought. This has important consequences for conservation planning, as the rate of destruction of rainforests in Madagascar has been one of the highest in the planet, with more than 80 percent of the historic surface of rainforest already lost, according to the study's authors. Almost a quarter of the new species discovered have not been found yet in protected areas, but the unstable political situation in Madagascar has also been cited as hampering conservation efforts. "Although a lot of reserves and national parks have been created in Madagascar during the last decade, the actual situation of politic instability is allowing the cut of the forest within national parks, generating a lot of uncertainty about the future of the planned network of protected areas", said Vieites. Madagascar is the fourth largest island in the world and one of the most biodiverse areas globally, with a high degree of endemic species. "To get an idea of its biodiversity --while in the Iberian Peninsula [there] are about 30 species of amphibians and in Germany about 20, in a single locality in Madagascar we can find around 100 species of frogs," said Vieites. Dr. Miguel Vences, professor at the Technical University of Braunschweig, Germany, who was also part of the study team, and believes that a century of new species discovery is just beginning: "People think that we know which plant and animal species live on this planet. But the majority of life forms on Earth is still awaiting scientific recognition."

Madagascar is already recognized as one of the world’s most important biodiversity hotspots, but an extensive reassessment of the island’s frogs suggests that its biological richness has been seriously underestimated. By combining broad field surveys with genetic, morphological, and acoustic analyses, researchers identified at least 129 and possibly as many as 221 previously unrecognized amphibian species. Adding these candidates to the species already described would raise Madagascar’s known frog diversity from roughly 250 species to between about 370 and 470.

Many of the newly identified frogs are “cryptic species”: animals that look similar to known species but are genetically distinct and may also differ in their calls, behavior, or ecological requirements. Traditional surveys based mainly on outward appearance can therefore group several separate species under a single name. The study’s use of DNA evidence, alongside anatomical observations and recordings of mating calls, revealed hidden diversity that conventional classification had overlooked.

The discoveries were not confined to remote or unexplored regions. Numerous candidate species were found in national parks and other areas that scientists had already studied intensively. This indicates that even relatively well-surveyed habitats may contain substantial undocumented biodiversity. More isolated forests and poorly explored regions could hold still more species.

The findings have implications far beyond Madagascar. Amphibians are among the most threatened groups of vertebrates, facing habitat destruction, climate change, pollution, invasive species, and emerging diseases. If similarly large numbers of cryptic species remain unidentified in other tropical regions, estimates of global amphibian diversity may need to increase dramatically—potentially approaching twice the currently recognized total.

At the same time, the research highlights an urgent conservation problem. Madagascar’s forests and wetlands are disappearing rapidly because of logging, agricultural expansion, fires, mining, and other human pressures. Many frog species occupy extremely small ranges, sometimes limited to a single mountain, forest fragment, or stream system. Such restricted distributions make them especially vulnerable: a species could decline severely or become extinct before it is formally described.

Protecting Madagascar’s remaining natural habitats is therefore essential not only for well-known animals such as lemurs, but also for hundreds of amphibian species that science is only beginning to recognize. Expanded surveys, faster taxonomic work, long-term monitoring, and stronger protection for both established reserves and unprotected habitats will be necessary to prevent this newly revealed diversity from disappearing almost as soon as it is discovered.

Researchers used genetic analysis alongside comparisons of the frogs’ appearance, habitats and calls to distinguish the newly identified animals from known species. However, the researchers say further work will be needed to formally describe and name each species — a process that can require detailed anatomical studies, additional DNA evidence and comparisons with museum specimens.

A species could be at risk of extinction before scientists have had a chance to formally document it.

# Madagascar’s frog diversity may be far greater than records show, study finds

**A major survey published in the journal *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences* suggests that Madagascar could harbor between 129 and 221 frog species previously unknown to science—potentially increasing the island’s recognized amphibian diversity by as much as 90%.**

Researchers reached the estimate after combining DNA analysis with traditional studies of anatomy, coloration, behavior and mating calls. Their work indicates that many frogs previously treated as members of widespread species are, in fact, genetically distinct lineages that may warrant recognition as separate species.

The study, titled **“Vast underestimation of Madagascar’s biodiversity evidenced by an integrative amphibian inventory,”** was led by David R. Vieites and an international team of amphibian specialists. It drew on roughly 15 years of fieldwork involving about 2,850 specimens collected from approximately 170 sites across Madagascar.

At the time of the research, 244 frog species were formally recognized on the island. Adding the candidate species identified by the team would bring the estimated total to between **373 and 465 species**.

## DNA exposes hidden diversity

The scientists used DNA barcoding—particularly comparisons of mitochondrial genetic sequences—to identify frogs that appeared similar but belonged to deeply separated evolutionary lineages. They then assessed those genetic results alongside physical traits, geographic distribution and, where available, the distinctive calls male frogs use to attract mates.

The researchers divided the newly detected lineages into different levels of certainty. At least 129 were considered strong candidate species, supported by multiple forms of evidence or substantial genetic differentiation. A broader interpretation produced an upper estimate of 221 possible new species, although some of those would require further study before they could be formally described.

That distinction is important: the paper did not formally name 221 new frogs. Instead, it identified a large pool of **candidate species**—populations likely to represent previously unrecognized species but still requiring detailed taxonomic examination.

The results show how conventional surveys can underestimate biodiversity when animals are classified primarily by outward appearance. Closely related frogs may evolve very different calls or genetics while retaining nearly identical body shapes and coloration, creating so-called cryptic species that are difficult to distinguish in the field.

## An island shaped by isolation

Madagascar is already recognized as one of the world’s most important biodiversity hotspots. Its long geographic isolation allowed plants and animals to evolve independently, producing exceptional levels of endemism. Nearly all of its native frog species occur nowhere else.

Many of those amphibians are associated with humid eastern rainforests, mountain streams or isolated highland habitats. Such specialization can generate large numbers of species with extremely small ranges, sometimes limited to a single forest, mountain or river system.

The study found that the hidden diversity was not evenly distributed. Some of the greatest uncertainty occurred in species-rich and taxonomically difficult frog groups, including several genera in which animals look broadly alike despite significant genetic differences.

Researchers cautioned that even their expanded estimate might not represent the final total. Some parts of Madagascar remain poorly surveyed, while certain frogs are highly seasonal, active only under particular weather conditions or difficult to detect because of their small size and secretive behavior.

## Conservation consequences

The findings carry serious implications for conservation. Species with narrow distributions are generally more vulnerable to habitat destruction than animals spread across broad areas. If what was once considered a single widespread frog is actually several locally restricted species, each may face a much greater risk of extinction than previously assumed.

Madagascar’s forests have been under sustained pressure from agricultural expansion, logging, charcoal production, mining and other forms of land conversion. Amphibians also face threats from climate change and emerging diseases, including chytrid fungal infections, which have devastated frog populations in other parts of the world.

The study reported that a substantial share of the candidate species occurred outside Madagascar’s existing protected-area network. That means some frogs may be threatened before scientists have formally named them or assessed their conservation status.

The discovery of cryptic species can also alter evaluations under the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List. A nominal species previously judged secure because of its wide range might need to be divided into several species, each occupying a much smaller area and potentially qualifying for a higher threat category.

## A case for “integrative taxonomy”

The researchers argued that the work demonstrates the value of integrative taxonomy, which combines genetics, morphology, acoustics, ecology and geography rather than relying on a single source of evidence.

DNA screening can rapidly flag unusual populations, but genetic differences alone do not always establish that two groups are separate species. Physical examination, mating calls and reproductive or ecological differences are needed to test many of the proposed classifications. Formal descriptions will therefore require additional fieldwork, museum comparisons and peer-reviewed taxonomic studies.

Even with those qualifications, the scale of the estimate is striking. An additional 129 species would increase Madagascar’s known frog fauna by more than half; an additional 221 would nearly double it.

The research suggests that one of the world’s best-known centers of amphibian diversity remains far from fully documented. It also adds urgency to efforts to protect Madagascar’s remaining forests: without faster surveys and habitat conservation, some of the island’s frogs could disappear before science has established that they exist.

counterfactuals.output:
The discovery of roughly 129–221 previously unrecognized frog species—potentially almost doubling Madagascar’s known frog fauna—suggests that global biodiversity has been substantially underestimated.

- **Global estimates:** David Vieites emphasized the scale of what remains unknown: **“People think that we know which plant and animal species live on this planet. But the century of discoveries has only just begun—the majority of life forms on Earth is still awaiting scientific recognition.”** If Madagascar’s hidden diversity is representative of other poorly surveyed tropical regions, worldwide amphibian totals—and broader species estimates—may need significant upward revision.

- **Faster, more integrated inventories:** Frank Glaw noted that traditional taxonomy alone can be slow: **“During the past 15 years, we have found and described more than 100 new species of frogs from Madagascar. This study shows that the pace of discoveries can be accelerated enormously using an integrative approach and cooperation among different experts.”** Combining DNA analysis, anatomy, field observations, and frog calls could therefore produce more realistic biodiversity assessments elsewhere.

- **Conservation priorities:** Miguel Vences warned that discovering species is not enough if protection is delayed: **“It would be terrible if we were to lose species before we even knew they existed.”** Newly identified frogs may have very small ranges, including forests outside existing reserves. Conservation planning must therefore account for candidate and undescribed species, expand surveys, reconsider protected-area boundaries, and protect habitats before every species has received a formal scientific name.

Overall, the finding implies both **more biodiversity than current global counts recognize** and **greater extinction risk than conservation plans currently capture**.

# Madagascar’s Hidden Amphibian Diversity Is Greater—and More Vulnerable—Than We Realize

Madagascar is celebrated for animals found nowhere else on Earth, from lemurs and tenrecs to vividly colored chameleons. Yet one of the island’s richest evolutionary stories is unfolding closer to the forest floor. Its frogs represent an extraordinary, and still underestimated, share of global amphibian diversity.

Nearly all of Madagascar’s native amphibians are endemic. Moreover, surveys, genetic studies and closer examination of museum specimens continue to reveal “cryptic” species: frogs that appear nearly identical but differ in their DNA, calls, behavior or ecological requirements. As a result, the number of recognized species is not a fixed total. Many frogs currently grouped under a single scientific name may eventually prove to represent several distinct species, each occupying a much smaller range than previously assumed.

Discoveries in well-studied reserves illustrate how much remains hidden. In Ranomafana National Park, a mountainous rainforest in southeastern Madagascar, researchers have documented remarkable frog diversity across streams, leaf litter and different elevations. Continued fieldwork has uncovered previously unrecognized populations and helped scientists distinguish species that are difficult to separate by appearance alone. The park’s steep terrain and varied microclimates create isolated habitats in which lineages can diverge over time.

A similar pattern has emerged in the rainforests of Mantadia National Park and the neighboring Analamazaotra reserve, often associated with the Andasibe-Mantadia protected area. These forests are famous for indri lemurs, but nighttime surveys also reveal a dense amphibian community. Tiny leaf-litter frogs, stream specialists and tree frogs can live within narrow ecological zones. Analysis of their calls and genetics has shown that even accessible, frequently visited forests may contain species not yet formally described.

These findings are encouraging, but they also expose a conservation problem. If Madagascar’s amphibian diversity has been underestimated, then the threats facing it have likely been underestimated as well.

Rainforest loss remains one of the greatest dangers. Forest is cleared or degraded by slash-and-burn agriculture, logging, charcoal production, mining and expanding settlements. Amphibians are particularly sensitive because many require cool, humid conditions, clean streams and intact vegetation. A forest patch may remain visible on a map while becoming too dry, fragmented or polluted to support its most specialized frogs.

Political instability can intensify these pressures. During periods of weakened governance and economic disruption, protected areas may face illegal logging, wildlife exploitation and reduced enforcement. Conservation programs can lose funding or access, while rural communities with few alternatives may become more dependent on forest resources. Political uncertainty also interrupts the long-term research needed to identify species, monitor populations and respond to emerging threats.

Protected areas such as Ranomafana and Mantadia/Analamazaotra are therefore essential—but they are not sufficient. Some newly recognized or still-unnamed frogs occur outside park boundaries, sometimes in a single forest fragment or watershed. Such species may disappear before scientists formally describe them. Others may be classified as widespread because several distinct species are still being treated as one, masking the vulnerability of each lineage.

Climate change and disease add further uncertainty. Shifts in rainfall and temperature can alter breeding cycles and shrink suitable habitat, especially for high-elevation species. Amphibian diseases, including chytrid fungal infections, remain a concern because small-range species could decline rapidly if exposed to a severe outbreak.

Protecting Madagascar’s amphibians will require more than naming new frogs. Priorities include preserving forest corridors, strengthening community-managed reserves, safeguarding streams, supporting local livelihoods and expanding surveys beyond famous national parks. Taxonomy and genetic research must also continue, because conservation decisions depend on knowing what species exist and where they live.

Madagascar’s frogs are easy to overlook, but they are sensitive indicators of forest health and irreplaceable products of millions of years of evolution. The discoveries in Ranomafana and Mantadia/Analamazaotra show that even celebrated protected areas still hold biological surprises. The greater danger lies beyond them, where unprotected species may be vanishing before the world learns their names.
